messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Nadia Haddad is a 75-year-old judge who came to treatment months after the sudden death of a loved one, speaking in the controlled, deliberate cadence that has shaped her years on the bench but breaking when she turns to the moment she cannot stop reviewing. She is married, and she describes a long life built around steadiness, judgment, and responsibility. It is precisely those qualities that now seem, in her mind, to indict her. When she tells the story, she returns again and again to what she did and did not do, as if the loss might still yield to closer examination. Her loved one died unexpectedly, and although she can recount the external facts, what dominates her account is her conviction that the death happened because of the way she acted. She has come to believe that if she had spoken differently, moved faster, noticed more, or insisted on something she now imagines she missed, the outcome would have been different.

Since the death, Nadia has interpreted her distress not as grief alone but as evidence of personal failure. She says, with visible shame, that her reactions since the event prove she is “a lousy coper.” She is unsettled by how often her mind returns to the loss, by how easily she becomes tearful in private, and by the fact that she no longer trusts her own composure. For a woman who has spent decades making decisions under pressure, she experiences these reactions as humiliating. She does not describe herself as someone wounded by a devastating event so much as someone exposed as inadequate by it. The meaning she gives her suffering is harsh and moralized: if she were stronger, more competent, more disciplined, she believes she would be handling this differently.

Her self-reproach is especially focused on protection. Nadia says she should have protected the person who died and failed. That belief carries the force of a duty violated. In session, she speaks as though her role in the family should have extended beyond love into prevention, as though vigilance and good judgment should have been enough to hold death back. She measures herself against an impossible standard and finds herself guilty each time. The fact that the death was sudden has not softened this conclusion; if anything, the unexpectedness seems only to deepen her sense that she should somehow have anticipated it. She circles around small details of timing, words exchanged, and choices made, searching them for the moment where she believes she abandoned her responsibility.

Her work as a judge remains the setting in which these beliefs are most painfully alive. On the bench, she can still conduct proceedings, but the role now feels altered from within. Cases involving families, loss, or questions of responsibility strike her with particular force, though she speaks of this carefully and without embellishment. More broadly, the courthouse has become a place where her identity as a decisive, reliable person is constantly placed against the private conviction that she failed where it mattered most. She notices every moment of hesitation in herself. A pause before ruling, a lapse in concentration in chambers, an evening when she comes home depleted rather than composed—each is taken by Nadia as further proof that her reactions since the death show weak character. She does not describe anger at fate or randomness. Instead, she repeatedly returns to the idea that something in her way of acting caused the tragedy and that her ongoing distress confirms the same deficiency.

At home with her husband, she is often quieter than she used to be, not because she lacks thoughts but because so many of them turn accusatory as soon as she tries to speak them aloud. She worries that if she says everything she believes about herself, it will sound irrational, yet privately she remains certain that she should have done more. What frightens her most is not only that she lost someone she loved, but that the loss has reorganized her understanding of herself into someone fundamentally unequal to crisis. By the time she sought help, she was exhausted by this unending internal prosecution. She said she wanted, if possible, to understand why she cannot stop holding herself responsible, but beneath that hope was a more painful fear: that therapy might confirm what she already suspects, that when the moment came to protect someone, she failed, and that nothing in the years she has spent being strong can outweigh that.
